records.topic: What If You Stood in Neptune's Winds?
records.hook: Why Neptune's winds reach 2,100 kilometres per hour.
records.openingLine: Why Neptune's winds reach 2,100 kilometres per hour.
records.secondBeat: They're the strongest sustained winds of any planet.
records.scientificMechanism: Neptune's deep atmosphere and internal heat drive the fastest sustained winds of any planet
records.scenarioChange: a visitor faced Neptune's cloud-top winds
records.expectedConsequence: winds several times faster than Earth's strongest hurricanes, at −218 °C
records.coreQuestion: If you stood in Neptune's winds, how fast would they blow?
records.misconception: The fastest winds aren't on the planets nearest the Sun; they're on distant, frigid Neptune.
editorialTitles: The Fastest Winds in the Solar System
Why Frozen Neptune Has Supersonic Winds

facts.claim: These weather patterns are driven by the strongest sustained winds of any planet in the Solar System, as high as 2,100 km/h (580 m/s; 1,300 mph).
Neptune's outer atmosphere is one of the coldest places in the Solar System, with temperatures at its cloud tops approaching 55 K (−218 °C).
Neptune orbits the Sun once every 164.8 years at an orbital distance of 30.1 astronomical units (4.5 billion kilometres).
At the time of the Voyager 2 flyby in 1989, the planet's southern hemisphere had a Great Dark Spot comparable to the Great Red Spot on Jupiter.
Temperatures at the planet's centre are approximately 5,400 K (5,100 °C).

narration.text: Why Neptune's winds reach 2,100 kilometres per hour.
They're the strongest sustained winds of any planet.
Yet its cloud tops sit near −218 °C.
Its centre is about 5,400 kelvin, driving the weather.
In 1989, Voyager 2 saw a Great Dark Spot there.
One Neptune year lasts 164.8 Earth years.
Standing in those winds, nothing on Earth could hold you.
So the coldest planets can have the wildest weather.

records.topic: What If You Flew Through Enceladus's Geysers?
records.hook: Why a 500-kilometre moon sprays over 100 geysers.
records.openingLine: Why a 500-kilometre moon sprays over 100 geysers.
records.secondBeat: Enceladus hides a liquid ocean under its ice.
records.scientificMechanism: tidal heating keeps a subsurface ocean liquid, and water escapes through cracks at the south pole
records.expectedConsequence: direct samples of an ocean hidden under ice
records.coreQuestion: If you flew through Enceladus's geysers, what would you find in the spray?
records.misconception: Small icy moons aren't necessarily dead; Enceladus sprays its hidden ocean into space.
visualScenes: plumes erupting from the south pole
cutaway of ice shell and ocean
Saturn's E ring fed by plumes
editorialTitles: The Moon That Sprays Its Ocean Into Space
What Cassini Found in Enceladus's Geysers

facts.claim: More than 100 geysers have been identified.
In 2014, NASA reported that Cassini had found evidence for a large south polar subsurface ocean of liquid water with a thickness of around 10 km (6 mi).
It is about 500 kilometres (310 miles) in diameter, about a tenth of that of Saturn's largest moon, Titan.
Enceladus was discovered on August 28, 1789, by William Herschel, but little was known about it until the two Voyager spacecraft flew by Saturn in 1980 and 1981.

narration.text: Why a 500-kilometre moon sprays over 100 geysers.
Enceladus hides a liquid ocean under its ice.
In 2014, Cassini found evidence of it near the south pole.
That ocean may be about 10 kilometres thick.
Saturn's tides keep flexing the moon, holding the water liquid.
Flying through a plume means sampling that ocean directly.
So the easiest alien ocean to study sprays itself into space.

records.topic: What If We Lived on Proxima b?
records.hook: Why a year on Proxima b lasts 11 days.
records.openingLine: Why a year on Proxima b lasts 11 days.
records.secondBeat: It hugs a dim red dwarf, 4.2 light-years away.
records.scientificMechanism: a planet in the habitable zone of a dim red dwarf must orbit very close, completing a year in days
records.scenarioChange: people settled on Proxima Centauri b
records.expectedConsequence: an 11-day year under a red sun, if the planet held onto air and water
records.coreQuestion: If we lived on Proxima b, what would a year and a sunrise be like?
records.misconception: The nearest known exoplanet isn't Earth 2.0; almost everything about it is still uncertain.
visualScenes: red dwarf star over a rocky planet
editorialTitles: What Life on the Nearest Exoplanet Would Be Like
Why Proxima b Has an 11-Day Year

facts.claim: The host star is the closest star to the Sun, at a distance of about 4.2 light-years (1.3 parsecs) from Earth, and is part of the larger triple star system Alpha Centauri.
It orbits Proxima Centauri every 11.185 Earth days at a distance of about 0.048 AU, over 20 times closer to Proxima Centauri than Earth is to the Sun.
It is probably a terrestrial planet with a minimum mass of 1.06 M🜨 and a slightly larger radius than that of Earth.
About 20–40% of all red dwarfs have one planet in the habitable zone.

narration.text: Why a year on Proxima b lasts 11 days.
It hugs a dim red dwarf, 4.2 light-years away.
It orbits over 20 times closer than Earth does to the Sun.
It's at least 1.06 times Earth's mass.
Its red sun would look larger but far dimmer than ours.
Whether it keeps air and water is still unknown.
Up to 40% of red dwarfs may host planets like it.
So the nearest new world is close, and still a mystery.

records.topic: What If Pluto Were Still a Planet?
records.hook: Why Pluto lost its planet status in 2006.
records.openingLine: Why Pluto lost its planet status in 2006.
records.secondBeat: The discovery of Eris in 2005 forced the question.
records.scientificMechanism: the 2006 planet definition requires clearing an orbit, which Pluto has not done in the Kuiper belt
records.expectedConsequence: dozens of similar Kuiper belt worlds would also need to count
records.coreQuestion: If Pluto were still a planet, how many planets would we have?
records.misconception: Pluto wasn't demoted for being small; it doesn't clear its orbit.
editorialTitles: Why Pluto Stopped Being a Planet
What If Pluto Were Still a Planet

facts.claim: In 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) formally redefined the term planet to exclude dwarf planets such as Pluto.
Doubts increased following the discovery of additional objects in the Kuiper belt starting in the 1990s, particularly the more massive scattered disk object Eris in 2005.
Light from the Sun takes 5.5 hours to reach Pluto at its orbital distance of 39.5 AU (5.91 billion km).
New Horizons was the first spacecraft to visit Pluto and its moons, making a flyby on July 14, 2015.
Pluto has a moderately eccentric and inclined orbit, ranging from 30 to 49 astronomical units from the Sun.

narration.text: Why Pluto lost its planet status in 2006.
The discovery of Eris in 2005 forced the question.
Eris is more massive than Pluto.
Planets must clear their orbits, and Pluto shares the Kuiper belt.
Keep Pluto a planet, and many Kuiper worlds would join it.
Sunlight takes 5.5 hours to reach it.
New Horizons flew past it in 2015.
So Pluto didn't shrink. Our definition grew up.

records.topic: What If the Strongest Earthquake Struck Today?
records.hook: Why Chile's 1960 quake flooded Hawaii 10,000 kilometres away.
records.openingLine: Why Chile's 1960 quake flooded Hawaii 10,000 kilometres away.
records.secondBeat: It measured 9.4 to 9.6, the strongest ever recorded.
records.scientificMechanism: a great subduction-zone rupture lifts the seafloor, launching a tsunami across an ocean
records.scenarioChange: a Valdivia-scale earthquake struck a modern coast
records.expectedConsequence: local destruction, then a tsunami hitting coasts 10,000 km away
records.coreQuestion: If the strongest earthquake ever recorded struck today, who would feel it?
records.misconception: An earthquake's reach isn't limited to its country; its tsunami can cross an ocean.
editorialTitles: The Strongest Earthquake Ever Recorded
Why Chile's Quake Hit Hawaii

facts.claim: Most studies have placed it at 9.4–9.6 on the moment magnitude scale, making it the strongest earthquake ever recorded.
On 22 May 1960, an earthquake and tsunami occurred in Chile, devastating the city of Valdivia.
It occurred in the afternoon (19:11:14 UTC, 15:11:14 local time), and lasted 10 minutes.
The main tsunami traveled across the Pacific Ocean and devastated Hilo, Hawaii, where waves as high as 10.7 metres were recorded over 10,000 kilometres from the epicenter.
The tremor caused localized tsunamis that severely battered the Chilean coast, with waves up to 25 metres (82 ft).
Various estimates of the total number of fatalities from the earthquake and tsunamis have surfaced, ranging between 1,000 and 6,000 killed.

narration.text: Why Chile's 1960 quake flooded Hawaii 10,000 kilometres away.
It measured 9.4 to 9.6, the strongest ever recorded.
The shaking lasted 10 minutes.
Waves up to 25 metres struck the Chilean coast.
In Hilo, Hawaii, waves reached 10.7 metres.
Today, coasts all around the Pacific would get warnings, and hours to act.
So the biggest quakes are ocean-wide events.

records.topic: What If One Volcano Grounded Every Plane?
records.hook: Why one volcano stranded 10 million travellers.
records.openingLine: Why one volcano stranded 10 million travellers.
records.secondBeat: In 2010, Iceland's Eyjafjallajökull sent ash across Europe.
records.scientificMechanism: volcanic ash melts in jet engines, so aviation authorities close airspace where ash spreads
records.scenarioChange: a volcanic ash cloud spread across a continent's airspace
records.coreQuestion: If one volcano grounded every plane, how long could a continent cope?
records.misconception: A modest eruption can disrupt more people than a giant one if its ash drifts into busy airspace.
visualScenes: ash plume over an Icelandic glacier
editorialTitles: The Volcano That Grounded Europe
Why Ash Is Deadly to Jet Engines

facts.claim: About 20 countries closed their airspace to commercial jet traffic, affecting approximately 10 million travellers.
The disruptions started over an initial period of six days in April 2010.
Beginning on 14 April 2010, the eruption created an ash cloud that led to the closure of most of the European IFR airspace from 15 until 20 April 2010.
Although no commercial aircraft were damaged, the engines of some military aircraft were harmed.

narration.text: Why one volcano stranded 10 million travellers.
In 2010, Iceland's Eyjafjallajökull sent ash across Europe.
About 20 countries closed their airspace to jets.
Most European airspace shut from 15 to 20 April.
Ash can melt inside jet engines and stop them.
Some military jet engines were damaged.
So a modest eruption can halt a continent's travel.

records.hook: Why 15% of northern land rests on frozen ground.
records.openingLine: Why 15% of northern land rests on frozen ground.
records.secondBeat: That's permafrost, and it's starting to thaw.
records.scientificMechanism: permanently frozen ground holds ice, carbon and foundations in place; thawing destabilises all three
records.expectedConsequence: sinking ground, damaged infrastructure and released carbon
records.coreQuestion: If the permafrost thawed, what would sink first?
records.misconception: Permafrost isn't lifeless; it holds microbes that wake up as it thaws.
editorialTitles: What Happens When Frozen Ground Thaws
Why Arctic Buildings Are Sinking

facts.claim: Around 15% of Northern Hemisphere land that is not completely covered by ice is directly underlain by permafrost; 22% is defined as part of a permafrost zone or region.
Estimates suggest nearly 70% of such infrastructure is at risk by 2050.
In 2014, regional estimates of alpine permafrost extent had established a global extent of 3,560,000 km2.
Microorganism numbers in permafrost soil typically range from 1 to 1000 million per gram of soil.

narration.text: Why 15% of northern land rests on frozen ground.
That's permafrost, and it's starting to thaw.
Alpine permafrost alone covers about 3,560,000 square kilometres.
As ice inside the ground melts, the surface slumps.
Nearly 70% of infrastructure on it may be at risk by 2050.
Each gram of frozen soil can hold up to 1,000 million microbes.
So thawing ground threatens both buildings and the climate.

records.topic: What If Magnets Could Make You Float?
records.hook: Why 1 frog floated in mid-air inside a magnet.
records.openingLine: Why 1 frog floated in mid-air inside a magnet.
records.secondBeat: Its body's water was pushed away by the field.
records.scientificMechanism: diamagnetic materials, including water in living tissue, are weakly repelled by strong magnetic fields
records.scenarioChange: a magnetic field was strong enough to lift a living animal
records.expectedConsequence: frogs and mice have been levitated; humans would need far stronger fields
records.coreQuestion: If magnets could make you float, how strong would they need to be?
records.misconception: Magnets don't only attract metal; every material responds, and water is weakly repelled.
visualScenes: live frog levitating in a magnet bore
editorialTitles: How Scientists Levitated a Frog
Why Water Is Pushed Away by Magnets

facts.claim: Diamagnetism was first discovered when Anton Brugmans observed in 1778 that bismuth was repelled by magnetic fields.
In 1845, Michael Faraday demonstrated that it was a property of matter and concluded that every material responded to an applied magnetic field.
Most spectacularly, a live frog was levitated.
In September 2009, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory announced it had successfully levitated mice using a superconducting magnet.

narration.text: Why 1 frog floated in mid-air inside a magnet.
Its body's water was pushed away by the field.
It's called diamagnetism, first seen with bismuth in 1778.
In 1845, Faraday showed every material responds to magnets.
In 2009, NASA's lab levitated mice the same way.
Lifting a human would need an enormous magnet.
So you're magnetic too, just very weakly repelled.

records.topic: What If You Lived Without Clocks?
records.hook: Why one man's days stretched to 48 hours.
records.openingLine: Why one man's days stretched to 48 hours.
records.secondBeat: Michel Siffre lived in caves without clocks or daylight.
records.scientificMechanism: without daylight and clocks, the body's circadian rhythm drifts away from 24 hours
records.scenarioChange: a person lived for months without time cues
records.expectedConsequence: the internal day stretches and the sense of elapsed time collapses
records.coreQuestion: If you lived without clocks or daylight, how long would your days become?
records.misconception: Your body clock isn't locked to 24 hours; daylight keeps resetting it.
visualScenes: caver alone underground with a lamp
editorialTitles: The Man Who Lived Without Time
What Happens to Your Body Clock Underground

facts.claim: He examined how humans experience time by spending 62 or 63 days without time cues, cloistered 130 m below the surface in the abyss of Scarasson, beginning July 1962.
In 1972, Siffre performed a more extensive underground experiment, staying six months in Midnight Cave in southern Texas.
After the experiment, he concluded that without time cues, he adjusted to a 48-hour rather than a 24-hour cycle.
Siffre underwent an additional cave excursion from November 1999 to February 2000, celebrating the New Year there but missing the actual date by three days.

narration.text: Why one man's days stretched to 48 hours.
Michel Siffre lived in caves without clocks or daylight.
In 1962, he spent 62 or 63 days 130 metres underground.
In 1972, he stayed six months in a Texas cave.
His body drifted to a 48-hour rather than 24-hour cycle.
Later, he missed New Year's Day by three days.
So daylight, not willpower, keeps your body on schedule.

records.topic: What If You Could Run Like Usain Bolt?
records.hook: Why 9.58 seconds still stands as the 100-metre record.
records.openingLine: Why 9.58 seconds still stands as the 100-metre record.
records.scientificMechanism: sprint speed depends on force applied to the ground and stride length, limited by muscle and tendon
records.scenarioChange: an ordinary person ran at a world-record pace
records.expectedConsequence: a 100 m dash in under 10 seconds, near the edge of human biology
records.coreQuestion: If you could run like Usain Bolt, how fast would you actually be going?
records.misconception: Bolt's 2009 record wasn't a tiny improvement; it was the biggest jump of the electronic-timing era.
editorialTitles: How Fast Usain Bolt Really Ran
The Limits of Human Sprinting

facts.claim: Bolt improved upon his second 100 m world record of 9.69 with 9.58 seconds in 2009 – the biggest improvement since the start of electronic timing.
He has twice broken the 200 metres world record, setting 19.30 in 2008 and 19.19 in 2009.
He has helped Jamaica to three 4 × 100 metres relay world records, with the current record being 36.84 seconds set in 2012.
He became the first junior sprinter to run the 200 m in under twenty seconds, taking the world junior record outright with a time of 19.93 s.

narration.text: Why 9.58 seconds still stands as the 100-metre record.
Usain Bolt ran it in 2009.
He cut his own record from 9.69 seconds.
It was the biggest jump since electronic timing began.
That same year, he ran 200 metres in 19.19.
Most people would need well over twice as long.
So world records show where human biology tops out.

records.topic: What If You Could See More Colours?
records.hook: Why half of women may carry 4 colour pigments.
records.openingLine: Why half of women may carry 4 colour pigments.
records.secondBeat: Most people see colour with three cone types.
records.scientificMechanism: colour vision depends on cone types; a fourth type could in principle add another colour dimension
records.scenarioChange: a person had four working colour channels
records.expectedConsequence: finer distinctions between shades most people see as identical
records.coreQuestion: If you could see more colours, what would the world look like?
records.misconception: Having a fourth photopigment doesn't guarantee seeing extra colours; the brain must use it.
editorialTitles: The People Who May See Extra Colours
What Tetrachromacy Really Means

facts.claim: Another study suggests that as many as 50% of women and 8% of men may have four photopigments and corresponding potentially increased chromatic discrimination.
Human rod cell sensitivity is greatest at 500 nm (bluish-green) wavelength, which is significantly different from the peak spectral sensitivity of the cones (typically 420, 530, and 560 nm).
Specifically, she has been shown to be a trichromat in the range 546–670 nm where people with normal vision are essentially dichromats.
If S cones of cDa29 provide independent color perception dimension as they normally do, that would confirm her being a tetrachromat.

narration.text: Why half of women may carry 4 colour pigments.
Most people see colour with three cone types.
Those cones peak around 420, 530 and 560 nanometres.
As many as 8% of men may carry a fourth pigment too.
But few people actually use it to see extra colours.
Those who do can split shades others see as one.
So colour is built in your brain as much as in your eyes.

records.topic: What If Quantum Computers Beat Every Supercomputer?
records.hook: Why 200 quantum seconds rivalled 2.5 billion years.
records.openingLine: Why 200 quantum seconds rivalled 2.5 billion years.
records.secondBeat: That was the claim for Google's quantum chip.
records.scientificMechanism: quantum processors sample from superpositions of many qubits, tasks that are hard to simulate classically
records.scenarioChange: quantum computers clearly outperformed classical machines on useful problems
records.expectedConsequence: breakthroughs in chemistry and materials; for now, claims keep shifting as classical methods improve
records.coreQuestion: If quantum computers beat every supercomputer, what would they actually be good for?
records.misconception: Quantum supremacy claims can shrink as classical algorithms improve.
visualScenes: quantum chip in a dilution refrigerator
editorialTitles: The 200-Second Calculation That Shocked Computing
Why Quantum Supremacy Keeps Moving

facts.claim: The paper states that to generate the number of samples the quantum computer generates in 200 seconds, a classical supercomputer would require 2.5 billion years of computation.
In 2024, the Google team estimated that, thanks to improvements in classical tensor network algorithms, simulating 53 qubits would take only six seconds on the Frontier supercomputer.
Google had announced plans to demonstrate quantum supremacy before the end of 2017 with an array of 49 superconducting qubits.
In October 2017, IBM demonstrated the simulation of 56 qubits on a classical supercomputer.

narration.text: Why 200 quantum seconds rivalled 2.5 billion years.
That was the claim for Google's quantum chip.
It used 53 qubits to sample random circuits.
By 2024, better classical methods cut the simulation to six seconds.
In 2017, IBM had already simulated 56 qubits classically.
Real payoffs would come in chemistry and materials design.
So quantum advantage is a moving target, not a finish line.

records.topic: What If Every Car Drove Itself?
records.hook: Why robotaxis have logged 200 million driverless miles.
records.openingLine: Why robotaxis have logged 200 million driverless miles.
records.secondBeat: Waymo gives about 500,000 paid rides a week.
records.scientificMechanism: robotaxis combine sensors, maps and software to drive without a human, one city at a time
records.scenarioChange: self-driving cars replaced human drivers everywhere
records.expectedConsequence: a slow city-by-city rollout, with mapping, regulation and edge cases as the limits
records.coreQuestion: If every car drove itself, how far along are we really?
records.misconception: Driverless cars aren't everywhere yet; they operate in mapped cities, expanding gradually.
editorialTitles: How Close We Are to Cars That Drive Themselves
Why Robotaxis Spread City by City

facts.claim: As of June 2026, Waymo operates public commercial robotaxi services in 10 US metropolitan areas, has 3,871 robotaxis in service, provides 500,000 paid rides per week, and has logged 200 million fully autonomous miles.
Google's development of self-driving technology began in January 2009, and the project was revealed in October 2010.
In October 2020, Waymo became the first company to offer service to the public without safety drivers.
By the end of 2015, Project Chauffeur had covered more than a million miles.

narration.text: Why robotaxis have logged 200 million driverless miles.
Waymo gives about 500,000 paid rides a week.
It runs 3,871 robotaxis in 10 U.S. metro areas.
Development began in 2009.
In 2020, it first carried the public with no safety driver.
Each new city needs mapping, testing and approval.
So self-driving arrives street by street, not all at once.

records.topic: What If a Cosmic Ray Hit Like a Baseball?
records.secondBeat: Physicists nicknamed it the Oh-My-God particle.
records.scientificMechanism: a single subatomic particle accelerated to extreme energy carries macroscopic amounts of kinetic energy
records.scenarioChange: a particle arrived carrying the energy of a thrown ball
records.expectedConsequence: a particle shower in the atmosphere, detected from the ground
records.coreQuestion: If a single particle hit with the energy of a baseball, where could it have come from?
records.misconception: Cosmic rays aren't all tiny energies; one particle once carried energy you could feel.
visualScenes: air shower cascading through the atmosphere
Fly's Eye detector in Utah desert
energy comparison with a thrown ball
editorialTitles: The Particle Physicists Named Oh-My-God
Why One Particle Carried So Much Energy

facts.claim: The Oh-My-God particle was an ultra-high-energy cosmic ray detected on 15 October 1991 by the Fly's Eye camera in Dugway Proving Ground, Utah.
As of 2026, it is the highest-energy cosmic ray ever observed.
Its energy was estimated as 320 exaelectronvolt.
Its energy was 20 million times greater than the highest photon energy measured in electromagnetic radiation emitted by an extragalactic object, the blazar Markarian 501.

narration.text: Why one particle carried 320 exaelectronvolts.
Physicists nicknamed it the Oh-My-God particle.
A detector in Utah caught it in 1991.
It remains the highest-energy cosmic ray ever observed.
It beat the top blazar photon energy 20 million times over.
That's roughly the energy of a thrown ball, in one particle.
So something in the universe accelerates particles beyond our machines.

records.topic: What If Our Sun Were as Big as UY Scuti?
records.hook: Why one star dwarfs the Sun 1,000 times over.
records.openingLine: Why one star dwarfs the Sun 1,000 times over.
records.secondBeat: UY Scuti is a red supergiant, 5,900 light-years away.
records.scientificMechanism: red supergiants swell to enormous radii late in life while their outer layers become thin
records.scenarioChange: the Sun swelled to the size of a red supergiant
records.expectedConsequence: its surface would engulf the inner Solar System
records.coreQuestion: If our Sun were as big as UY Scuti, which planets would be inside it?
records.misconception: The biggest stars aren't the heaviest; red supergiants are huge but diffuse.
visualScenes: UY Scuti beside the Sun to scale
Solar System orbits inside a supergiant
editorialTitles: The Star 1,000 Times Wider Than the Sun
What If the Sun Became a Red Supergiant

facts.claim: UY Scuti is a red supergiant or hypergiant star, located 5,900 light-years away in the constellation Scutum.
They determined that all three stars are over 1,000 times bigger than the Sun and over 100,000 times more luminous than the Sun.
The analysis was based on an old radius of 1,708 R☉.
Potentially larger radius estimates have already been published for other supergiant stars, such as VX Sagittarii, NML Cygni, MY Cephei, and Stephenson 2 DFK 1.

narration.text: Why one star dwarfs the Sun 1,000 times over.
UY Scuti is a red supergiant, 5,900 light-years away.
It shines over 100,000 times brighter than the Sun.
An older estimate put its radius at 1,708 Suns.
Put it in our Sun's place, and the inner planets would be inside it.
Its outer layers are so thin, they're nearly vacuum.
So the biggest stars are giants in size, not in density.

records.hook: Why over 90% of plants depend on fungi.
records.openingLine: Why over 90% of plants depend on fungi.
records.secondBeat: Fungal threads wrap roots and trade nutrients for sugar.
records.scientificMechanism: fungi partner with plant roots and break down dead matter, recycling nutrients
records.expectedConsequence: most plants lose root partners and dead matter piles up
records.coreQuestion: If all fungi disappeared, what would happen to plants and forests?
records.misconception: Fungi aren't just mushrooms; most of their work happens underground with plant roots.
visualScenes: species count chart known versus estimated
editorialTitles: What If Fungi Vanished Tomorrow
The Hidden Network Keeping Plants Alive

facts.claim: Over 90% of plants are dependent on Mycorrhizal symbiosis between plants and fungi and this process also enhances photosynthesis in plants.
The true biodiversity of the fungus kingdom has been estimated at 2.2 million to 3.8 million species.
Only about 148,000 have been described, with over 8,000 species known to be detrimental to plants and at least 300 that can be pathogenic to humans.
In August 2021, the IUCN Species Survival Commission asked that the phrase fauna and flora be replaced by fauna, flora, and funga.

narration.text: Why over 90% of plants depend on fungi.
Fungal threads wrap roots and trade nutrients for sugar.
There may be 2.2 to 3.8 million fungus species.
Only about 148,000 have been described.
Without them, most plants would struggle to feed.
Dead leaves and wood would pile up, barely rotting.
So forests stand on a network you rarely see.
